review.headline: A Vienna Gambit where you survived a worse position, missed a forced mate, and then lost on time while winning

sections.text: White chose the Vienna Gambit with 3.f4 and you met it with 3...d6 and 4...dxe5. After 5.Nf3 Nbd7?! and 6.Bc4 Bb4 White had a small lead in development, and 7...Bxc3?! 8.bxc3 Nxe4 won a pawn but left you a little worse.
9.Qe2? was a mistake, but your reply 9...f5?? was a blunder, because 9...Nd6 was the safe move. White did not take full advantage, but 10.Ba3 b6? left you around -4, and you needed White to err.
The game turned on the kingside. After 13.gxf5 gxf5! and 14.Nxe5?? you played 14...Qg5+? when 14...Rg8+ was better. After 15.Kh1?? the quiet 15...Nf2# was a forced mate, but you played 15...O-O-O?.

You still had a winning position. 17...Ng3+! was a fork of the queen on e2, the rook on f1 and the king on h1, and after 18.Kg2 Nxe2 you were up a queen. You went on to lose on time in a position that was totally winning.

review.turning_point: 15.Kh1?? allowed 15...Nf2#, a forced mate. You played 15...O-O-O? instead, though you still got a winning attack with 17...Ng3+!.
review.focus: After 14.Nxe5 the checks 14...Rg8+ and, a move later, 15...Nf2# were the key. Start every attacking move by listing all the checks, then manage the clock.

review.headline: A six-move Petrov miniature: one blunder, one check, one queen

sections.text: You went into the Petrov Damiano line with 3.Nxe5. Your opponent replied with 3...Nxe4 and you brought out the queen with 4.Qe2, a well-known idea that puts the queen on the e-file opposite the king.
Black went wrong at once with 4...Nf6??, retreating the knight off the e-file. The correct answer was 4...Qe7, which would have kept the balance.

You found the shot with 5.Nc6+!. That is a discovered check, because the knight leaves e5 and uncovers your queen on e2 against the king on e8. Black has to deal with check and cannot save the queen on d8, which the knight on c6 also attacks.
After 5...Be7 you simply took with 6.Nxd8 and were up the queen, around nine points of material. This was a model finish and a great reminder of the 4.Qe2 trap.

review.turning_point: 5.Nc6+! was a discovered check that won the queen after 4...Nf6??.
review.focus: Nothing to fix here. Keep the habit of looking for checks when the queen faces the king along a file, as you did on move 5.

review.headline: A quiet Giuoco Pianissimo that was decided by a single tactic on the f-file

sections.text: You played a calm Italian with 4.d3 and 5.Be3, offering a trade of bishops. After 5...Bxe3 6.fxe3 you got the semi-open f-file, a useful feature for the rest of the game.
You developed with 7.O-O and 8.Nc3, then posted the knight on d5 with 9.Nd5. 10.Qe2?! was a small inaccuracy; 10.h3 was cleaner. Even so the position stayed balanced.
12.Nxf6+ Qxf6 13.Nd4 set a trap that your opponent fell into. 13...Bxc4?? took a bishop but left the queen on f6 facing your rook on f1 along the open f-file.
14.Rxf6! won the queen for a bishop, and your opponent resigned. Great use of the open file you made on move 6, and good calm play before the tactic.

review.turning_point: 13...Bxc4?? took a bishop but 14.Rxf6! won the queen on the open f-file.
review.focus: Your only inaccuracy was 10.Qe2?!, where 10.h3 kept the knight on g4 at bay. Look at whether a quiet pawn move can solve the problem before you move the queen.
